title: The River Crossing

full_text:
Returning from an auspicious pilgrimage to a distant temple, Guru Paramartha and his five faithful disciples arrived at the sandy banks of the broad Palar river. The river was shallow, its crystal-clear water flowing gently over smooth white pebbles, scarcely reaching a man's knees.

Yet as they prepared to wade across, Madayan suddenly seized the Guru's robes, his eyes wide with superstitious terror: 'Halt, revered Master! Do not touch the water! Do you not know that rivers are living, sentient beings, and that this river is currently wide awake and fiercely vigilant?'

The Guru stopped, stroking his beard: 'Is it awake, Madayan? How do we determine whether a river is awake or asleep?'

Madayan expounded his profound theory: 'When a river is awake, Master, its spirit watches for travelers to drag down and swallow! But when a river falls asleep, its spirit closes its eyes, its waters become docile, and travelers may step across without the slightest peril! We must test whether the river is sleeping!'

'How shall we test it?' asked Matti.

Madayan instructed: 'Fetch a blazing firebrand from that roadside campfire. Thrust the fiery brand into the water. If the river is awake, it will shriek and bite; but if it is asleep, it will remain silent!'

Peedan ran to the fire, seized a thick, blazing wooden branch, and ran to the water's edge. With all his might, he thrust the glowing, red-hot brand into the cool river!

The contact of fiery coal with cold water produced a sharp, violent hiss: 'TSSS-SH-SH-SH!' accompanied by a cloud of white steam.

Peedan dropped the brand, leaped three yards backward, and shrieked in horror: 'IT BIT! IT HISSED! THE RIVER IS AWAKE AND ROARING WITH FURY!'

The Guru and his disciples retreated into the shade of a banyan tree, trembling with fear. 'We must wait,' proclaimed the Guru solemnly, 'until the river falls into a deep, peaceful slumber!'

For six long hours under the blazing sun, the six philosophers sat upon the hot sand, watching the water. Whenever a wave lapped against the bank, Madayan whispered: 'Hush! It stirs in its bed! Do not disturb it!'

At noon, an old, weary donkey carrying two heavy bags of salt wandered down the bank. Being thirsty, the donkey stepped boldly into the river, waded into the middle of the current, drank its fill, and walked calmly to the opposite bank without the slightest difficulty.

Watching the donkey cross unharmed, Matti leaped up: 'Look, Master! Look! The river is asleep! The donkey crossed without waking it!'

The Guru nodded with immense gravity: 'The donkey, being a simple beast, crossed softly. But we are men of heavy scholarship! We must cross with extreme stealth, so that our footsteps do not awaken the sleeping monster!'

Guru Paramartha and his five disciples removed their sandals, tied their robes around their necks, and began crawling across the shallow river on their hands and knees, tiptoeing on all fours like stealthy cats, holding their breath in terrified silence!

Whenever water splashed against their chins, they glared at each other, hissing: 'Shhh! Do not wake the river!'

Halfway across, Peedan sneezed: 'ACHOO!'

The disciples shrieked in terror: 'IT WAKES! RUN FOR YOUR LIVES!'

Panicked, they scrambled through the shallows, splashing water in all directions, tumbling over each other, and dragged themselves onto the opposite bank, soaked, muddy, and exhausted, collapsing on the sand.

Turning around, the Guru looked back at the river and proclaimed in triumph: 'We have outsmarted the sleeping river through our supreme stealth! Let all future philosophers study our glorious crossing!'

The village washermen watching from the bank broke into thunderous laughter, while the disciples cheered their master's tactical genius.
moral: Do not invent imaginary perils out of foolish superstition; test the water before you declare the river asleep.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The River Crossing"?
options: Foolishness of book knowledge without worldly wisdom
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
